map_note.t: Alaska elects one at-large U.S. House member. Under the system voters adopted in 2020 (first used in 2022), all candidates run on one open primary ballot regardless of party, and the top four advance to a ranked-choice general election. The 2026 primary was Aug 18; the general is Nov 3. Results were certified and the withdrawal deadline passed at 5 p.m. on Aug 31, when about 20 candidates withdrew, letting lower finishers move up. Senate: fourth-place Democrat David Leslie withdrew, so fifth-place Republican Gerald Heikes advanced. Third-place Dan J. Sullivan (no relation to the senator) declined to withdraw; the Division of Elections had disqualified him in June, but the courts restored him. House: Democrats Matt Schultz, John B. Williams and Yaquelin Reynoso and Republican Clay Strickland withdrew, which moved Democrat Eric Hafner and eighth-place Libertarian Jim McDermott onto the ballot. Governor: second-place Democrat Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and sixth-place Click Bishop withdrew. Fifth-place Treg Taylor was next in line, but on Aug 31 Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom declined to certify him after the Alaska Public Offices Commission voted 4–1 that his candidate financial disclosure (missing tenant names) was not filed on time. His running mate, Candice English, took the slot with Jodi Taylor as her running mate. Late on Sept 4, Dahlstrom reversed herself, citing an informal Department of Law review, and certified Taylor. General-election ballots began mailing Sept 18.

research_notes: FINAL BALLOT SOURCE: the Alaska Division of Elections general-election candidate list (elections.alaska.gov/candidates/?election=26genr) and sample ballots could not be fetched; the fetch tool refused them on provenance/permission grounds. The final ballot here is therefore verified from news and secondary sources instead: Alaska Public Media/KTOO (Sep 2), Alaska Beacon (Aug 31, Sep 5), Alaska's News Source (Aug 31, Sep 5), Wikipedia, The Green Papers, and the Tanana Chiefs Conference snapshot (last modified Oct 8, 2026). All agree on the four names in each race.

TAYLOR RUNNING MATE — UNRESOLVED: During the Aug 31–Sep 4 disqualification, Candice English moved up to governor and named Jodi Taylor (Treg Taylor's wife) as her lieutenant governor. After the reinstatement, the Alaska Beacon/KTOO say Taylor 'replaces' English, while quoting Taylor saying 'Candi and I are running.' The Tanana Chiefs snapshot (Oct 8) and Wikipedia list Taylor/Candice English. An ADN/Journal of Commerce headline (Sep 9; page blocked) says English is 'set to remain in governor's race alongside Taylor's wife.' The exact lieutenant-governor name printed on the ballot needs a human check against the official sample ballot.

Dan Sullivan Jr. court dates conflict across sources. Disqualification: the AP says Director Carol Beecher's determination was dated June 15; Wikipedia gives a preliminary decision June 10 and a final decision June 16; a Beacon photo caption says June 12. Superior Court reversal: Green Papers says June 25, Wikipedia June 26. The Alaska Supreme Court order was June 29 (Green Papers; Beacon link date).

Dan Sullivan Jr.'s ballot name is given as 'Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.' (Tanana Chiefs, Green Papers) and his label as blank/no party (AP; Green Papers on the July 24 sample ballot). The Alaska Public, Beacon and NPR pieces call him 'Dan J. Sullivan' and do not use 'Jr.'
Senate Wikipedia article has not been updated with 2026 primary results; Senate primary percentages come from The Green Papers and the Alaska Beacon.
House ratings: Cook (Likely R, Sep 25, 2026) was read directly. The Inside Elections and Sabato ratings (Likely R) are from Wikipedia and dated Oct 2025, so they may be stale.
Governor ratings (Cook, Inside Elections, Sabato) are from Wikipedia and were not checked on the forecasters' own pages.
Campaign sites and FEC ids come from The Green Papers; neither the sites nor the FEC pages were opened in this pass. Heikes and Hafner have no listed campaign website.
Photos not researched in this pass; photo fields are blank, not guessed.

Write-ins (not on the printed ballot, so not in candidates): Senate — Sidney 'Sid' Hill and Heather McElwain; Governor — James 'JP4' Parkin IV (running mate Ramadhani Greer). Source: The Green Papers.
Peltola's 2022 start date and the exact start of Taylor's attorney-general tenure (Wikipedia: 2021–2025) were not checked against a primary record.

AK-SEN.note: Peltola led the Aug 18 top-four primary 49.5% to Sullivan's 41.4%. A second Dan Sullivan, a Petersburg retired teacher unrelated to the senator, is on the ballot with no party label: the Division of Elections tried to disqualify him, and the courts restored him. The senator's camp calls that candidacy a sham, which the candidate and Peltola deny.

candidates.name: Dan Sullivan

oneliner.t: Two-term Republican senator, first elected in 2014 over Democrat Mark Begich and re-elected in 2020; endorsed by Donald Trump and Sen. Lisa Murkowski; second in the Aug 18 top-four primary with 41.4%.

He finished third with 2.5%. The senator's campaign and the NRSC call the candidacy a sham meant to confuse voters; he and Peltola's campaign deny any coordination.

candidates.name: Gerald Heikes

oneliner.t: Palmer Republican and perennial candidate who says he is running to Sullivan's right. He finished fifth with 1.1% and moved onto the November ballot when fourth-place Democrat David Leslie withdrew.

AK-GOV.note: Open seat with one Democrat (Kreiss-Tomkins, 22.5% in the primary) against three Republicans (Wilson, Bronson, Taylor). Republican leaders failed to get the GOP field to consolidate, and Taylor and Wilson have taken different positions on how Republicans should rank. Taylor was removed from the ballot on Aug 31 and restored on Sept 4.

candidates.name: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins

oneliner.t: Former Democratic state representative (2013–2023) who led the primary with 22.5%. Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed him, leaving him the only Democrat. Running mate for lieutenant governor: Zac Johnson, an Anchorage Assembly member registered nonpartisan/independent.

candidates.name: Treg Taylor

oneliner.t: Former Alaska attorney general (2021–2025) who finished fifth (7.3%) and moved into the final four when Tom Begich withdrew. The Lt. Governor declined to certify him Aug 31 after APOC voted 4–1 that his financial disclosure, which listed tenants of his apartment building only by first name and last initial, did not substantially comply with the law by the deadline; she reinstated him Sept 4, citing an informal Department of Law review. His running mate is Candice ‘Candi’ English, per the Division of Elections’ candidate list as reported by the Juneau Independent.

oneliner.t: Republican incumbent since January 2025, who won the seat in 2024 with 51.2% over then-Rep. Mary Peltola. Trump endorsed his 2026 bid, and he led the primary with 44.6%.

candidates.name: Eric Hafner

oneliner.t: Democrat with no apparent Alaska ties, serving a federal prison sentence in New York (release projected for 2036) after pleading guilty in 2022 to making threats against police officers, judges and others. He also made the 2024 general ballot over an Alaska Democratic Party challenge, and drew 3.8% in the 2026 primary.
